page.title: Instagram photos and hashtags
page.kicker: Lecture 07 · week 4, day 1 · running case: Instagram
page.dek: Upload and serve photos the way Instagram and GitHub do with pre-signed URLs and a CDN, then build a hashtag page with counting on Kafka.
page.description: Lecture 07: how a CDN works, uploading photos with pre-signed URLs, storing only what you can't derive, signed URLs and private photos, then Instagram's hashtag page with batched counting on a re-partitioned Kafka topic.

chapters.title: Instagram's first year
chapters.summary: Fourteen million users, three engineers, and a stack every later startup copied. What Instagram ran, and how tech stacks spread.

chapters.title: A CDN as a black box
chapters.summary: One building block that changes almost every public-facing system. What a CDN does, configured and traced request by request, as an engineer uses it.

chapters.title: Uploading a photo
chapters.summary: 5 million photos a day. Where they live, why they should never pass through your API servers, and the pre-signed URL every image upload is built on.

chapters.title: Storing the post
chapters.summary: The column almost everyone adds to the posts table, why it is the one to leave out, and how a post finds its photo without it.

chapters.title: Who can see a private photo?
chapters.summary: A CDN knows nothing about followers, so what makes a private account private, and what would real privacy cost?

chapters.title: Extend and optimize
chapters.summary: Tell every other service that a post exists, and let the CDN shrink a 50 MB photo for a phone on a slow network, both by reusing what already exists.

chapters.title: The hashtag page: what to store
chapters.summary: A page that looks too simple to design. What it shows, who owns which part, and the one document that renders it in a single read.

chapters.title: Counting hashtags
chapters.summary: count++ on every post is how a database drowns. Batch it, and discover why batching forces a second Kafka topic.

chapters.title: The whole hashtag design
chapters.summary: The top 100 arrives from another team without a single synchronous call, the page is served from a CDN, and the read path / write path method checks every hop.

chapters.title: Running the pipeline
chapters.summary: The questions that come after the diagram: Kafka goes down, a new consumer joins, the SLA tightens, someone wants Kafka as a database, and the servers run hot.

chapters.title: What to keep
chapters.summary: The habits behind both features, one CDN used three ways, and where the next lecture picks up.
